item.title: Art of the Game or the Loss of the Gamble?
item.description:
Addiction

Art of the Game or the Loss of the Gamble?

Personal Perspective: Gambling and gaming may sound different, but they are not.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Gambling and gaming are easier than ever.
  • Wins and losses exponentially affect mood. All the agency belongs to the result of the gamble.
  • Researchers have studied the decision-making process involved and found a focus on the wins despite losses.
  • If addiction is suspected, partners should assume control of finances to protect themselves and children.

My father was a gambler. He did not see his behavior as reckless. He had many highs and as many lows. I felt every one.

His gambling took different forms. He defied legal advice and, when I was thirteen, lost everything. We abruptly moved across the country to live with my older sister and her husband. She had endured similar rocky times alongside my brother when they were young. I’m hesitant to say that what I lived through was worse, but I know this much is true: Dad’s recklessness had progressed alongside his denial.

My father covered up his shame of loss through brooding and sadness, and my mother expressed hers through neediness and unrelenting anger, including anger at me. They had a combustible relationship after we moved, and the intensity barely diminished for decades, right up until the day he died.

Dad was both a hard worker and dreamer, a valuable combination in work and life, but it was his propensity toward the belief that he would beat the odds and “overcome” no matter what he did that led to trouble. Distorted thinking and illusion of control—these traits apply to most addictions. But gambling is the meth of money problems—and unfortunate is the one who dips their toe in and is sucked in up to their neck. In fact, even the family treatment approach departs from most other addictions in one key area: detachment from resources. It is advised that, once a partner finds out about the gambling debts, they separate the finances when possible, and that the nonaddicted spouse take complete control of the money—debit cards, credit cards, paychecks—before they, too, are swallowed up in the downward spiral of debt and can’t stop it. The velocity of loss adds to the treacherous nature of this particular addiction.

In recent years, gambling has gotten a glamorous makeover. Today it’s known as gaming. Video game-like apps allow for seamless phone wagers and joining bets with others. It all looks so easy, so normal, and so fun. For a great history of this slow, methodical rebranding, see Danny Funt’s Everybody Loses: The Tumultuous Rise of American Sports Gambling.

Jody Bechtold, LCSW, ICGC-II, BACC, is a gambling addiction expert and co-author of The Gambling Disorder Treatment Handbook: A Guide for Mental Health Professionals. In a course I recently completed for my clinical license renewal, I saw my experience validated in her book and felt a more mature sadness for the pressure my father felt and for his helplessness.

Bechtold writes about frequent mood swings that the gambler/gamer exhibits, including irritability, restlessness, or agitation. These often occur, she notes, when individuals attempt to cut down or stop gambling. I have seen this also occur when money is lost in significant amounts or when appreciation for gains is not met with the same enthusiasm the individual feels.

article continues after advertisement

Another characteristic I’ve noticed in people who gamble—or game—is how they distance themselves from loved ones, suddenly leaving the room to be alone, perhaps to check on scores or investments, to see what their wager is doing, and if they’ve won or lost. My father would spend a lot of time on the phone or away, taking long drives presumably for work—but who really knows?

In 2021, researchers wrote in The International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health “that the experience of gambling behavior in itself is a dynamic experience of events in time series, where gamblers anchor on the most recent event—typically a small loss or rare win.” They note that “this is a highly adaptive, but erroneous, decision-making mechanism, where anchoring on the most recent event alters the psychological representations of substantial and accumulated loss in the past to a representation of negligible loss. In other words, people feel better while they gamble.”

In the Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, researchers note that even if a long string of losses prevails before a win, the gambler will see their value. “With this restructuring, even games of (objectively) negative expected value, such as those at casinos, may be subjectively positive. The steeper the delay discounting, the greater the subjective value of the gamble (over normal ranges of discounting steepness). Frequent gamblers, who value gambles highly, would thus be expected to discount delayed rewards more steeply than would nongamblers.”

article continues after advertisement

Both studies validate my understanding that, even when my father was losing, he believed he could eventually be winning. This was not based on reality—that we were nearly homeless, for example—but on the “bet,” hope, and authentic desire that he would do better; that he would win. It’s sad, really, how this lightened his mood, but only very temporarily. He had no real agency in the matter, so feeling good was in correlation to the win.

We live in a society with free will and capitalism with porous guardrails. I sometimes wonder if my father were alive now, what he would do with a cell phone and the apps on it that provide a direct line to the promise of a winner’s high.

Fate intervened. He died at 74 on an upward trend. Cell phones at the time were a rarity. And his balance sheet was in the positive.

I don’t know what would have happened had he lived longer.

item.title: How Nature Helps Us Return to Ourselves
item.description:
Environment

How Nature Helps Us Return to Ourselves

Even brief time outside can restore perspective, attention, and calm.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Nature can help us step out of pressure, rumination, and constant self-monitoring.
  • The benefits of nature do not always require wilderness or long periods outdoors.
  • A healthier life may begin with noticing what is already alive around us.
The point is not to turn nature into another task. We do not need to optimise our walk, photograph every flower, count every step, or convert the experience into data. The point is simpler: to be there.
Source: Brendan Kelly

There is a particular feeling that comes from stepping into a green place. It might be a forest path, a city park, a garden, a canal walk, or a shaded lane where branches meet overhead and the light changes ahead.

Nothing dramatic has happened. No problem has been solved. The inbox is still there. The bills are still there. The news is still there. And yet something shifts.

The mind, which had been gripping tightly, loosens slightly.

The World Becomes Bigger

Modern life narrows attention. Screens narrow it. Deadlines narrow it. Worry narrows it. Even self-improvement can narrow it. Nature widens attention again.

A path through trees asks very little of us. It does not require performance. It does not ask for a password. It does not rate our productivity. It simply offers movement, texture, light, shadow, sound, and air.

This matters psychologically. Much distress involves a loss of proportion. A difficult email becomes the whole morning. A disappointment becomes a verdict. A worry becomes a world. Nature does not remove these things, but it can place them in a larger frame.

A tree is not in a hurry. A bird is not checking notifications. A path does not demand that we improve ourselves before we are allowed to walk on it.

Brief Contact Matters

A recent systematic review and meta-analysis examined nature exposure and mental health in adults with mental illness or symptoms of mental illness. Being outside for as little as 10 minutes, even in urban nature, can improve adults’ mental health. Shorter repeated exposures appear especially helpful.

This is an important message. We do not need to romanticise nature or imagine that only mountains, oceans, or wilderness count. A small pocket of green can matter. A tree-lined street can matter. A bench in a park can matter. A few minutes in daylight can matter.

This is not a cure-all. Nature is not a substitute for proper treatment when someone is seriously unwell. It does not erase poverty, trauma, loneliness, grief, or illness. But it can be part of care. It can be part of prevention. It can be part of recovery.

article continues after advertisement

What Nature Restores

Nature may help because it changes the kind of attention we use. Much of daily life demands directed attention: concentrate, respond, decide, remember, plan, hurry. This kind of attention is necessary, but it is tiring.

Natural environments often invite a softer form of attention. Leaves move. Light flickers. Water sounds. Birds appear and disappear. The mind has something to rest on, but not something it must dominate.

This can be deeply restorative. We are still conscious, but less stressed. We are still thinking, but less trapped by thought.

Nature also restores scale. Human problems are real, but they are not the only reality. There are roots, seasons, weather, insects, clouds, decay, growth, and renewal. The natural world reminds us that life is not only achievement. It is also process.

A Modest Prescription

A nature prescription need not be grand. Step outside for 10 minutes. Walk without headphones. Notice three colours. Look at the shape of a leaf. Sit near a tree. Watch the light change. Let the phone stay in your pocket.

The point is not to turn nature into another task. We do not need to optimise our walk, photograph every flower, count every step, or convert the experience into data.

The point is simpler: to be there.

item.title: Arts Engagement in Trauma Recovery Can Benefit Mental Health
item.description:
Creativity

Arts Engagement in Trauma Recovery Can Benefit Mental Health

Community arts programs can support healing, connection, and mental health.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Arts participation builds emotional and social resilience.
  • Trauma-informed arts programs are an effective addition to clinical care.
  • Creative engagement can strengthen mental well-being, social connection, and long-term trauma recovery.

Written by Thi Ngoc Mai Le, Graduate Research Assistant at the International Arts + Mind Lab, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine

“Path with Art gave me my life back. My spark. My love for life.”

For one participant of Path with Art (PwA), a Seattle-based nonprofit organization that provides free community arts programming for individuals affected by trauma, these words capture the power of community arts engagement. Rooted in the understanding that art is a fundamental human need, PwA provides free community arts programming, partnering with hospitals, shelters, and recovery organizations to make creative expression accessible to populations that are often considered “hard to reach.” These include people recovering from trauma such as homelessness, domestic violence, substance use disorders, and post-traumatic stress.

Community art-making at Path with Art
Source: Path with Art / Used with permission

Through storytelling, music, dance, poetry, and other creative practices, PwA, like community-based arts programs across the country, helps participants make meaning, build connection, and foster healing. Stories like these are common among participants, teaching artists, and community leaders who have long witnessed the transformation power of community-based programs. However, despite a growing body of research that has demonstrated the benefit of arts engagement, community arts programs remain understudied in the literature.

To help address this gap, the International Arts + Mind Lab at Johns Hopkins University partnered with Path with Art to examine the impact of community arts participation on mental wellbeing, social connectedness, and self-efficacy. These psychosocial outcomes were chosen as they have been shown to contribute to the trauma recovery processes. By combining both quantitative and qualitative methods, the study sought to measure not only outcomes but also to better understand the lived experience of participants and the mechanisms through which creative engagement may contribute to healing and recovery.

This 12-month study collected data from PwA participants after their 8-week art classes. The data collected included pre- and post-validated measures as well as an exit survey with open-ended questions to gain additional insight into their experiences in the PwA programs.

Study findings

The findings were positive and striking: More than 90 percent of participants reported increased self-efficacy—the belief that they can accomplish goals despite adversity. Nearly 90 percent self-reported improvements in mental health. More than 80 percent reported feeling less lonely, and nearly seven in ten said they made new friends. In addition, the three validated mental health survey tools found similar outcomes. They measured a significant increase in well-being, an increase in self-efficacy, and a significant reduction in loneliness.

article continues after advertisement

Participants viewed the PwA classes as a way to alleviate social isolation while also providing a safe, inclusive, and diverse community. They also emphasized how making art helped them manage stress and other trauma-related symptoms. Making art within a structured and communal environment also helped participants become more optimistic, hopeful, and positive. Participating in PwA classes also helped individuals discover and develop their own creative capacities, self-confidence, self-compassion, and self-awareness in an environment that encourages collaboration and experimentation.

Specific to the low-to-no income, trauma-impacted populations that were studied, PwA’s teacher-led classes provided participants with a unique sense of structure, dependability, stability, and support. Participants described the classes as a lifeline that helped them reconnect with meaning, motivation, and self-worth as well as helping them process their complex emotions.

Where do we go from here?

By gaining a deeper understanding of how arts programming influences trauma recovery, mental well-being, and social connectedness, community-based arts can become a holistic approach to support trauma recovery and be implemented more widely into our current health care systems as a complement to standard care.

Healing from trauma requires rebuilding trust, identity, purpose and connection. Art in a trauma-informed setting offers a uniquely powerful way to support recovery and rebuilding. This study provides important evidence and support for community-based arts programs that can be carried out in tandem with clinical, trauma-informed services.

item.title: What I Learned When I Ditched My Smartphone for a Year
item.description:
Social Media

What I Learned When I Ditched My Smartphone for a Year

Personal Perspective: Reflections on my year with limited screen time.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Ditching smartphones and social media for a year reduced my compulsive checking and dopamine-driven urges.
  • Stepping back from constant connectivity improved my real-world relationships.
  • Limiting news and social media exposure lowered my anxiety and social comparison.
  • The tradeoff is inconvenience and social disconnection.
Source: Photo by Girl with red hat on Unsplash

A year ago, I deleted my social media accounts and switched to a so-called dumb phone.

I made the move because I felt like social media wasn’t making me happier. It felt like a time suck. And even when I got rid of social media, I was still tethered to my smartphone. I caught myself checking my work email at all hours of the day and scrolling through my news feed. I felt like I wasn’t in control of the media streaming into my brain, regardless of the app blockers and time limits I tried to set for myself.

What I’ve noticed after a year without social media or a phone connected to the World Wide Web is that I’m no longer tethered. I rarely check my phone, and I definitely don’t stress when it’s running low on batteries.

I Feel Physically Free from a Device

The biggest change I’ve noticed since ditching my smartphone and social media is that I’m no longer reliant on a device. I don’t constantly check my phone because it rarely has any new information for me. I probably get four text messages a day and at least half are spam.

There’s no more dopamine rush urging me to check and recheck my phone. My phone is boring. When I don’t have anything to do, I’m much more likely to sit around and do nothing than to check my phone.

I Have More Time for Other Things

With my screen time going down to around zero, I have plenty of time for other things. I read. I write. I play with my kids.

I still use my laptop when I’m home, but it’s more cumbersome and not something I chronically pick up to check the news. I’m more likely to use it to write an article or do a bigger project.

I Feel More Regulated, More Often

I definitely noticed I would get snippy when someone interrupted my phone scrolling. Ditching that device with social media has helped me keep a slightly more even-tempered mood.

I’m more likely to be more present, which helps me navigate situations as they arise.

I Improved My Relationships with Real People

Because I’m detached from my phone, I can pick up more of the bids that my friends and family are making to connect with me. Snubbing people because of your phone is called “phubbing,” and now that my phone isn’t a draw, I’m much less likely to ignore or half-listen to them. I can be more present with and for them, which is great for improving relationships, real relationships.

article continues after advertisement

I Feel Less Anxious about the World

Now that I’m not doomscrolling, I feel a lot less stressed about current events. I still check the news when I’m feeling up to it, but having it comprise such a small percentage of my life has really cut down on my overall sense of doom and gloom. I spend a lot more time thinking about my family and community and a lot less on global events that don’t impact my immediate world as much.

I Compare Myself Less to Others

Now that I’m off social media, I compare myself to others a lot less. I don’t see people’s fancy vacations and latest renovations. I don’t see their hardcore morning routine or starvation diets. That means I do a lot more comparing myself to me. I’m running my own race much more often.

Source: Photo by Girl with red hat on Unsplash

I Feel Out of the Loop Sometimes

On the other hand, I do feel much more out of the loop now that I’m off social media and not constantly plugged in. I used to know about all the latest slang and trends. Now, they pass me by, and I’m left in the dark when people chatter about the latest viral craze. I know fewer and fewer celebrities and pop culture milestones. I’m OK with all this because I don’t feel like these things impact me all that much.

I have noticed that I’m also out of the loop about acquaintances' lives. I can’t scroll through their social media feeds, so I find myself catching up with people in real life when I see them. I didn’t see your vacation photos, so you need to start at the very beginning and catch me up.

I Have to Work Extra Hard in Our App-Ubiquitous Culture

Another downside of not having a smartphone is that they’ve become ubiquitous in our society. I’m supposed to have a phone that can scan QR codes and access museum maps, download apps to store boarding passes and concert tickets, and access apps to operate my car and find the nearest charging stations.

article continues after advertisement

I have to work extra hard to overcome some of these hurdles. If venues don’t offer paper menus or maps, I have to just ask a lot of questions. I have to print things from my home computer as much as possible and request key fobs to use charging stations.

These obstacles were why I actually switched back to a smartphone after blocking web surfing and email on it. It's technically a smartphone, but I turned it into a dumb smartphone that can't access the internet but can access my playlists and help me get from point A to point B.

I Am Staying the Course

I’m still keeping the internet and social media out of my pocket because the benefits outweigh the obstacles.

Sure, I’m not as easily reached. But I’m OK with that. I like that my life feels a lot more like it did when I was a teenager. I feel unencumbered and free to roam. I feel more present in the world. I feel a sense of clarity, like sometimes it’s okay to just stare at the wall or not have access to an answer.

Life feels more uncertain in some ways, which is exactly how I want it to feel. I’m in charge of what I watch, when I watch it, and how I spend my downtime. I feel like I can actually hear myself think again and that I’m much more in charge of my decisions. I’m less a robot and more myself.

I may not pick up when you call. You may not have heard from me in a while. I probably won't respond to your email right away. But know that I’m doing well. I’m out in the world, exploring, and figuring things out, my way.

item.title: No Evil, No Bad Parts: Sociological Support for IFS
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

No Evil, No Bad Parts: Sociological Support for IFS

Looking at Internal Family Systems through a sociological lens could open paths to healing.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • IFS encourages us to look at our relationships with others and contextualize them.
  • We are all subject to our responses to the harm and trauma we experience. The differences between us are few.
  • Bridging sociology and IFS has many positive possibilities.
  • Sociologically locating one’s Self gives us a path toward healing.

Dr. Richard C. Schwartz’s work developing the Internal Family Systems (IFS) model of therapeutic practice has become increasingly popular (e.g., Schwartz, 2021). Celebrities like Alanis Morissette, Jonathan Van Ness, and Sarah McLachlan have publicly praised the approach, citing its unique abilities to heal trauma and build connection, clarity, and compassion. Numerous clinicians, therapists, and life coaches have offered their own versions of IFS, with specificities around various topics such as motherhood (Close, 2026), eating (Catanzaro, 2026), and addictions (Sykes et al., 2023).

After reading dozens of IFS iterations, I found myself connecting deeply with these approaches—not only because IFS is a groundbreaking trauma-informed set of practices, but also due to its inherently sociological elements.

In this first post in a series of three, I offer sociological support for IFS by discussing opposition to “bad” or “evil” framings of human behavior and psychology. In doing so, this collective series aims to offer support for IFS and expands into a deeper understanding of its parameters as related to the field of sociology.

Source: Ann H / Pexels

No Such Thing as Evil

In my 20+ years of teaching (Worthen, 2022), I have encouraged my students to see the sociological constructions of deviance—including how certain individuals are at greater risk of being labeled as "deviant" based on gender, sexuality, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic class, etc—and how each of us is deviant in at least some time, location, and/or culture. While I conceptualize this framework through the lens of empathy, Schwartz grounds his (similar) work in the “no bad parts” motto.

Both approaches recognize that there is no such thing as “bad” or “evil” parts or people. We are all subject to our responses to the harm and trauma we experience. The differences between us are few. What is essential is that we learn how we engage with our inner selves and heal amidst the difficulties that we will all face as human beings.

During my initial read of No Bad Parts (Schwartz, 2021), I found myself penning sociological concepts and ideas in the margins. One was a note I wrote about psychologist Philip Zimbardo’s Stanford Prison Experiment (1971) and one of his books, The Lucifer Effect (Zimbardo, 2008). Ever since I learned about the Stanford experiment in my undergraduate psychology class, Zimbardo’s claims that “good” people can turn “evil” has troubled me.

article continues after advertisement

My interpretation of the study's events was much different than his. I didn’t feel that Dave Eshelman, often described as the most abusive and sadistic “guard," was becoming “evil” due to the power he was arbitrarily given. Instead, I suspected that it was likely something about the other “guards” and their collective influence that led to their horrendous treatment of the “prisoners.” I didn’t know it at the time, but I was thinking sociologically.

Source: Ron Lach / Pexels

Fast forward to when I began teaching sociology: I took an unconventional approach to The Stanford Prison Experiment to teach my students about differential association theory. First developed by criminologist Edwin Sutherland in 1939, the basic premise behind this theory is that the techniques, motives, and rationalizations of criminal behavior are learned and reinforced within intimate personal groups, most often amongst delinquent peers. The more persuasive group members are toward criminal behavior, the more likely each will participate in crime (Sutherland, 1939).

Differential association theory was later adapted by criminologist Ronald Akers into a more comprehensive theory about social learning which considers the processes of learning crime/criminality via imitation, differential reinforcement, and pro-criminal definitions (Akers, 1998).

After learning about these sociological/criminological theories and then reviewing The Stanford Prison Experiment, my students tend to quickly come to the conclusion that this experiment was less about individual psychology and the processes of becoming a “lucifer,” and more about the collective influence groups and group experiences can have on behavior. In other words, together my students and I conclude that there is no “evil”—only situations that can push people into coping with traumatic experiences through violence.

article continues after advertisement

I will admit that when I first picked up No Bad Parts, I was highly skeptical. I did not believe that anyone could fully convince me that rapists, child molesters, and murderers aren’t at least a little “bad.” But Schwartz’s (2021) firsthand accounts of his therapeutic practices with these types of people did convince me. In fact, I found myself realizing that I already believed this to be true.

In my teaching, I discuss motivations for rape and I encourage my students to blur the boundaries between us (law abiding, non-violent people) and them (criminals, rapists, murderers), and see that there is no such thing as an “evil lucifer.” More generally, the main takeaways in my sexual deviance course are:

  • What we think of as "deviance" is, in itself, neither inherently bad nor good; it is a social construct.
  • Sexual deviants, then, are also neither inherently bad, nor good, but rather the socially constructed stigmas attached to certain people, behaviors, and identities categorize them as such.
  • Sexual deviants are just like you and me—in fact, they are you and me.

The IFS model highlights these elements by working to expose the humanity in us all in efforts to heal trauma and live as our true Self—no evil, no bad parts, no bad people.

Sociocultural scripts about what is right/wrong sometimes push us into thinking we are somehow fundamentally “bad” and that something is wrong with us. We bury those parts down until they become exiles and we attempt to keep those exiles at bay through other parts, like managers and firefighters.

But if we get curious about our Self, we can unburden our trauma. If we do the work that IFS methods outline, we can understand why we feel the way we do, what the context of those feelings is, heal, and live as our true Selves. As psychologist Jesse Bering writes in his book Perv: The Sexual Deviant in All of Us:

“It’s not easy, but digging into the darkest corners of our sexual nature (that is to say our ‘perversions’) can expose what keeps us from making real moral progress whenever the issues of equality and sexual diversity arise. With each defensive layer we remove, the rats therein will flee at the daylight falling at their feet, and the opportunity to eradicate such a pestilence of fear and ignorance makes the excavation of our species’s lascivious soul worth our getting a little dirty along the way” (Bering, 2013, pp. 6–7).

article continues after advertisement
Source: Boom Photography / Pexels

Sociology and IFS

Sociological thinking is already embedded into the framework of IFS. Schwartz and others ask us to consider how our elements from our childhood, especially trauma through our relationships with others, may have shaped our difficulties in our adulthood. Highlighting the significance of family structure, Schwartz writes “context is everything” (2021; p. 61).

In other words, your Self is understood best when it is contextualized. By pushing us to look within—at our parts—IFS is simultaneously encouraging us to look at our relationships with others and contextualize them within larger sociocultural constructs including racism, classism, sexism, patriarchy, colonialism and many other infrastructures that cause us harm.

Thinking about our Self in society, that is, sociologically locating one’s Self, gives us a path toward healing from the inside out. In closing, bridging sociology and IFS has many positive possibilities. Contextualizing your feelings (perhaps another “C”) is one of them.
